headings.title: Why Referencing Matters in Nursing
headings.content: Referencing is the practice of acknowledging the original authors when you use their ideas, data, or words in your own writing. In nursing and healthcare, research directly impacts human lives. When you write a care plan, an essay, or a research project, your claims cannot rely on guesswork. Referencing proves that your clinical assertions rest on solid, peer-reviewed evidence rather than personal opinion. It also allows other nurses, educators, and researchers to trace your sources, verify your facts, and explore the topic further.

headings.title: Academic Integrity and Plagiarism
headings.content: Academic integrity means acting with honesty and responsibility in your scholarly work. **Plagiarism** is the serious ethical violation of taking someone else's work, words, or ideas and passing them off as your own. In nursing school, plagiarism can range from copying a paragraph word-for-word without quotation marks to buying an entire research project online. Even accidental plagiarism—such as forgetting to add a citation because you rushed your assignment—carries severe penalties, including failing a course or expulsion from the nursing programme. Safe academic habits require you to always separate your own thoughts from external sources while drafting.

headings.title: In-Text Citations Versus Reference Lists
headings.content:
A complete referencing system has two parts that work together: in-text citations and the reference list.

- **In-Text Citations**: Brief pointers placed inside the body paragraphs right where you use the source information. They usually contain the author's last name and the year of publication (e.g., Smith, 2021), pointing the reader directly to the full source.
- **Reference Lists**: A detailed list appearing at the very end of your paper. It provides full publication details—such as complete book titles, journal names, volume numbers, and digital object identifiers (DOIs)—so anyone can easily locate the exact material.

headings.title: Major Referencing Styles in Healthcare
headings.content:
Different academic disciplines prefer different formatting rules for citations. Healthcare education relies primarily on a few specific styles:

1. **APA (American Psychological Association)**: Most common in nursing, psychology, and social sciences. It emphasizes author-date in-text citations (e.g., Adebayo, 2022).
2. **Vancouver Style**: Common in medicine and biomedical journals. It uses sequential superscript numbers in the text (e.g., Adebayo¹), matching a numbered reference list.
3. **Harvard Style**: Another author-date system very similar to APA, though minor punctuation and formatting details differ.
4. **Chicago Style**: Often used in history and humanities, utilizing footnotes or author-date formats.

headings.title: Formatting APA In-Text and Reference Entries
headings.content:
Mastering basic APA format prevents common formatting deductions. For a **paraphrased** idea, include the author and year in parentheses, like (Okafor, 2020). For a direct quotation, you must also include the page number, such as (Okafor, 2020, p. 15). 

When building your reference list at the end of the paper, arrange items in alphabetical order by the first author's last name. Journal entries require the author, year of publication, article title, italicized journal name, volume number, issue number, and page range. Always use a **hanging indent** on reference entries, where the first line stays flush against the left margin and subsequent lines are indented.

headings.title: Citation Tools and Avoiding Common Mistakes
headings.content: Managing dozens of references manually can become overwhelming during major research projects. Reference management software—such as Zotero, Mendeley, or EndNote—can store PDFs, organize citations, and automatically generate reference lists in APA or Vancouver style. However, software is not infallible; it can pull incorrect metadata from poorly formatted web pages, resulting in capitalisation or italicisation errors. Students must always review software-generated citations against official style guides. A common misconception is that changing a few words in a copied sentence clears you of plagiarism; true paraphrasing requires completely rewriting the concept in your own voice while retaining the original citation.
